Ocean tides are caused primarily by the gravitational pull of the Moon, and to a lesser extent the Sun, on Earth's water. The Moon's gravity tugs the oceans toward it, creating a bulge of water on the side of Earth facing the Moon, while a second bulge forms on the opposite side due to inertia as the Earth is pulled slightly toward the Moon more than the far-side water is. As Earth rotates through these bulges, coastal areas experience the rise and fall we call high and low tides. When the Sun, Moon, and Earth align during full and new moons, their combined gravitational pull produces especially large "spring" tides, whereas smaller "neap" tides occur when the Sun and Moon pull at right angles to each other.
